seo.title: Karmic tail 3 19 16 compatibility in the destiny matrix
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 19 16 compatibility: The Empress, The Sun and The Tower — the home two people want, the light they live in, and the truth they must rebuild it on.

title: The 3-19-16 karmic tail in compatibility: a doll's house in the sun
short: The 3-19-16 tail in compatibility opens with the two brightest cards in the deck, The Empress and The Sun, and ends with The Tower, the card of collapse. The answer to the riddle is that this couple's Tower does not strike at love. It strikes at the stage set: a home where the two of them were merry, but not always truthful.

sections.h2: A Doll's House: the play that acts out the 3-19-16 tail in order
paragraphs: Ibsen finished the play in September 1879 in Amalfi, on the Italian coast. It came out in Copenhagen on 4 December, and by 21 December the Royal Theatre was already staging it. It is quoted here in R. Farquharson Sharp's English translation (1910). The action covers three days of Christmas. Torvald Helmer has just been made manager of a bank, and his wife Nora can, for the first time in years, buy presents without counting every coin.

Nora has a secret. In the first year of their marriage Torvald overworked himself and came close to death, and the only hope was a long stay in the south. There was no money, so Nora secretly borrowed 4,800 crowns and forged the signature of her father, who was dying at the time. The year in Italy saved her husband's life, and ever since she has been paying off the debt herself, in instalments. Torvald believes his father-in-law paid. The man who holds Nora's bond, Krogstad, works at the very same bank, and the new manager means to dismiss him. So Krogstad drops a letter with the whole truth into the Helmers' letter-box.

The three acts look like the three cards. In the first, the home: the tree is hidden from the children until evening, the table is covered in parcels, the husband calls his wife his lark and his squirrel. In the second act the sun is already burning low: in the corner stands the Christmas tree, "stripped of its ornaments and with burnt-down candle-ends on its dishevelled branches", and Nora rehearses the tarantella she learned on Capri. In the third, the letter has been read, and the house comes down.

The story did not come from nowhere. An acquaintance of Ibsen's, the writer Laura Kieler, secretly borrowed money when her husband was told to move to a warmer climate, and later committed forgery to pay it back. In real life the ending was harsher than on the stage.

The play is usually read as one woman's story. For a couple's tail something else matters more: the Helmers' house was built by two people, and it fell on both of them at once. In 1898, at a banquet given by the Norwegian Association for Women's Rights, Ibsen himself declined the honour of having worked for the women's cause: "I am not even clear what the women's cause really is. To me it has been a question of humanity" (our translation). So from here on, Nora and Torvald are not "she" and "he" but two roles. In a 3-19-16 couple either partner can take either role, and often both take turns.

sections.h2: The Empress at the entry: the home people keep quiet for
paragraphs: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a common language. The point sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also turn into resistance. For a 3-19-16 couple the entry holds The Empress, the card of fertility, abundance and home.

The play's first scene is The Empress in its pure form. Nora comes in loaded with parcels, has the tree hidden until evening, gives the porter a whole crown instead of fifty øre and tells him to keep the change, eats a macaroon or two on the way and wipes her mouth before her husband looks in. From the study comes: "Is that my little lark twittering out there?" Nora explains why they can spend a little: "This is the first Christmas that we have not needed to economise." Three children, a new salary, a pretty home — everything two people dream of at the entry.

This couple's common language is tender and toy-like: "lark", "squirrel", "little spendthrift", "Miss Sweet Tooth". It carries an agreement: one plays and the other admires; one spends and the other hands out money and shakes his head. There are no words in this language for a serious conversation.

There is also a rule, and Torvald states it in the first minutes: "No debt, no borrowing. There can be no freedom or beauty about a home life that depends on borrowing and debt." The original is sharper still: such a home gets "something unfree, and therefore something unlovely" about it. The home has to be beautiful, and beautiful means free of debt. But this home stands precisely on a debt, and Nora keeps quiet about it for beauty's sake: "It would upset our mutual relations altogether; our beautiful happy home would no longer be what it is now."

That is how the entry turns into resistance. The shared wish for a lovely home keeps the truth out of it. In Waite's list of divinatory meanings The Empress opens with "Fruitfulness, action, initiative", and in the same list, after a semicolon, comes "the unknown, clandestine". The initiative in the Helmer home is clandestine. Benebell Wen writes of The Empress: "She produces. She makes things happen." And in the same breath she warns that the card "might also be a foreshadowing of unintended or unanticipated consequences affecting that fruition." Her example, as it happens, is the Tour de Nesle affair, which puts a tower right inside The Empress card.

In a couple today this looks ordinary. Two people dream of a renovation, a trip, a nursery, a big family round the table. One is paying off a loan the other knows nothing about: "I didn't want to spoil the holidays." The other says nothing about a job that is wobbling, because things at home are so good. Both are protecting the home, and both are already laying silence into its foundations. Lisovskaya lists growing out of childishness among The Empress's tasks for a couple, and among her advice, learning to make decisions alone. In the doll's house decisions are made alone, but in secret, while the childishness is played for show.

sections.h2: The Sun in the middle: a year in Italy, bought on credit
paragraphs: The middle of the task is how the couple lives the road from the wish to the main task. Lisovskaya gives this point no meaning of its own; it only adds to the main task, and this reading is our adaptation. For a 3-19-16 couple the middle is The Sun, and in the play it is literal.

"It was a wonderfully beautiful journey, and it saved Torvald's life. But it cost a tremendous lot of money, Christine." Only the south could save her husband, and a year under the Italian sun did save him. The price is exact: 1,200 specie-dollars, 4,800 crowns. And this couple's sun is paid for in instalments. Nora pays the interest every quarter, spends only half of what her husband gives her for dresses ("Thank Heaven, any clothes look well on me, and so Torvald has never noticed it"), and last winter she took in copying work: "I locked myself up and sat writing every evening until quite late at night."

Ibsen names the card himself, and he gives the word to the one person who does not know who paid. On learning that their friend Dr Rank will soon die, Torvald says: "He, with his sufferings and his loneliness, was like a cloudy background to our sunlit happiness." Sharp's "sunlit" is word for word: the original has vor sollyse lykke. Wen describes The Sun in relationships in almost the same colours: "It indicates a radiant marriage, perhaps one to a spouse with a successful career", "It could suggest a power couple." The new bank manager and his merry wife at their first rich Christmas are exactly that couple.

In a couple The Sun also has a shadow. Lisovskaya lists among its tasks an inability to talk about problems, inflated expectations and taking credit for a partner's victories. In the play all of this is one situation. Torvald does not know his wife saved him and is sure his father-in-law paid. Nora is proud of what she did only in a whisper, in front of a friend: "I have not told you the important thing… It was I who saved Torvald's life."

The expectations are the worst part. Both secretly wait for a disaster in which a heroic deed will shine. Torvald confesses: "I have often wished that you might be threatened by some great danger, so that I might risk my life's blood, and everything, for your sake." Nora spends three days waiting for "the wonderful thing", meaning that her husband will read the letter and take the forgery on himself: as she tells him later, "I was so absolutely certain, you would come forward and take everything upon yourself, and say: I am the guilty one." Both expect a heroic deed against a backdrop of catastrophe, and neither says a word. This is The Sun at its minus: waiting for heroism instead of talking.

The card also leaves a clue in the numbers. Neither partner has The Sun in their personal centre or personal tail: only the couple gives birth to it. And in 44% of these couples The Sun is literally made of the tail's other two cards: one partner has The Tower (16) in the middle of their personal tail, the other has The Empress (3), and 16 + 3 = 19. This couple's Sun is built from a home and a blow from the very start, just as the year in Italy was built from care and a forged signature.

sections.h2: "No, only merry": a light kept on stage
paragraphs: This couple's Sun has a second face: the stage. The Neapolitan fisher-girl costume for the ball upstairs comes from the same sunny year: "Torvald had it made for me there." So does the dance: "the Tarantella that I learned at Capri." The sunny year has become a costume and a turn for the guests. Listing the names given to The Empress, Waite calls her "the woman clothed with the sun", an image from Revelation. In the Helmer home the sun has also become clothing: it is put on for the party.

The turn is a success, and Torvald leads his wife away at its peak: "as they say in novels, the beautiful apparition disappeared. An exit ought always to be effective, Mrs Linde." The day before, there was a rehearsal. Nora dances so that her husband never reaches the letter-box, and Torvald cannot bear it: "My dear darling Nora, you are dancing as if your life depended on it." — "So it does." He calls out "Slower, slower!" and "Not so violently, Nora!" The gaiety here is a way to put off The Tower for one more day.

Then comes the verdict on The Sun, the most exact line in the play. Torvald is indignant: "Have you not been happy here?" Nora: "No, I have never been happy. I thought I was, but it has never really been so." — "Not — not happy!" — "No, only merry." In the original, bare lystig: jolly, festive, in high spirits. Waite gives The Sun upright as "Material happiness, fortunate marriage, contentment", and reversed as "The same in a lesser sense." Merriment is exactly happiness in a lesser sense: the joy is real, it is simply used to cover what nobody talks about.

Hence the central question of the middle of the 3-19-16 tail: are the two of them happy, or only merry? From outside the two states look the same. The couple throws wonderful parties, shares jokes, has lovely holiday photos. And in eight years there has not been a single conversation about money, fears or wishes left unmet.

sections.h2: The Tower as the main task: a letter behind glass
paragraphs: The main task is the main point of the tail: the couple's chief trials. It is read mostly through the minus: what the two of them fail at and what they have to learn. For a 3-19-16 couple it is The Tower.

Waite writes of The Tower: "It is a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe." In the play the catastrophe is foreseen, and that is its peculiarity. Krogstad drops the letter, and Nora calls her friend to the door: "Do you see that letter? There, look — you can see it through the glass in the letter-box." — "And your husband keeps the key?" — "Yes, always." For three days both live next to a bolt of lightning visible through glass. The Tower of a 3-19-16 couple is often like that: they know about it in advance and dance so that it does not happen today.

The evidence that ruins Nora is a date. Her father died on 29 September, yet the signature on the bond is dated 2 October: he "signed this bond three days after his death." Ibsen builds the exposure on a number, the way the destiny matrix builds a tail on dates of birth. Wen writes of The Tower as if she had read the play: "What seemed stable and solid to the Seeker is not so; it is in fact destructible." The doll's house was destructible from the day a secret debt moved into it.

Lisovskaya lists among The Tower's tasks for a couple the collapse of an invented image of the partner, the loss of self-control, and two people looking in different directions when trouble comes. The third act shows all three. Torvald reads the letter: "What a horrible awakening! All these eight years — she who was my joy and pride — a hypocrite, a liar — worse, worse — a criminal!" His lark has fallen. Soon Nora will say: "I saw you were not the man I had thought you were." Her knight has fallen. Two images come down in one evening, and at that moment the two of them look in different directions: he thinks of his reputation, she of the wonderful thing. Waite calls The Tower the ruin of a House of Falsehood, and the doll's house fits the description without any strain.

sections.h2: Saving the shine: how a couple fails The Tower
paragraphs: After the first blow Torvald proposes a plan: "it must appear as if everything between us were just as before — but naturally only in the eyes of the world… From this moment happiness is not the question; all that concerns us is to save the remains, the fragments, the appearance —"

In the original the last word is skinnet. The Norwegian Academy's dictionary derives it from Old Norse skin, from skína, "to shine", and gives two senses. The first is light, gleam, hence solskinn, "sunshine". The second is an outward show that covers an inner flaw: appearance. The dictionary illustrates the second sense with exactly this line from A Doll's House. So after the blow Torvald wants to save the shine, the same root as in "sunshine". What remains of The Sun is a glow without warmth, a light for other people.

Then the second letter arrives: Krogstad returns the bond. "I am saved! Nora, I am saved!" — "And I?" — "You too, of course." The word "saved" has been heard in the play before, in the first act, about the trip south: "it saved Torvald's life." Both times he is saved by someone else's act, and both times someone else pays. He throws the bond into the stove — "The whole thing shall be nothing but a bad dream to me" — and promises that "soon everything will be just as it was before." From now on he will protect Nora "like a hunted dove", since "I have broad wings to shelter you under."

This is the 3-19-16 tail's main failure. The lightning has struck, and the couple hurries to rebuild the same house from the same drawings: the same roles, the same language, only with more protection. Wen writes that after The Tower the realisation "leads to rebuilding and reconstruction." Reconstruction is not restoration. In a couple today the failure looks like this: a debt, a lie or a secret comes out, the two make up quickly, book a trip, post a photo together, and never talk about why the secret was needed.

sections.h2: "Yes, Torvald, I have changed my things": The Tower at its strongest
paragraphs: Nora goes into the next room: "Taking off my fancy dress." It is the same Italian costume she danced in. Torvald is still talking through the door about his wings when she comes back "in everyday dress": "Yes, Torvald, I have changed my things now." — "Sit down. It will take some time; I have a lot to talk over with you."

For the third act Ibsen has already moved the table to the middle of the room, with a lamp burning on it. At this table the real Tower takes place, and it is not a shout or a slammed door but a sentence: "We have been married now eight years. Does it not occur to you that this is the first time we two, you and I, husband and wife, have had a serious conversation?" Nora announces: "Torvald, this is a settling of accounts." In the original, Dette er et opgør: a reckoning, a final having-it-out. The bill that was paid off in secret for years is laid on the table for the first time.

The strong version of The Tower for a 3-19-16 couple is a change of clothes. The sunny costume comes off, everyday clothes go on, and the two sit down at the table facing each other. For Lisovskaya, The Tower at its plus means trials passed together, after which the union is only stronger. A trial like that begins with an admission, and Nora makes it before any accusation: "You don't understand me, and I have never understood you either — before tonight."

Then Nora speaks about herself: "I have another task I must undertake first. I must try and educate myself." Lisovskaya advises a couple with The Empress that each partner should build a life of their own and learn to decide alone. Here the advice sounds like the main condition: two dolls will not make a married couple until each becomes a grown-up in their own right. So the question at the strong Tower is not "whose fault is it?" but "what have we never talked about?"

sections.h2: "The most wonderful thing of all": the ending Ibsen left open
paragraphs: Torvald asks whether he will ever be anything more than a stranger to her. Nora answers: "Ah, Torvald, the most wonderful thing of all would have to happen." — "Tell me what that would be!" — "Both you and I would have to be so changed that… That our life together would be a real wedlock." In the original Ibsen sets two Norwegian words side by side: samliv, living together, and ægteskab, marriage. The wonderful thing Nora waited three days for was someone else's heroic deed. The most wonderful thing of all is a change in both.

The play ends with two stage directions. Ibsen writes et håb skyder op i ham, "a hope shoots up in him"; Sharp has "A hope flashes across his mind." And straight after: "The sound of a door shutting is heard from below." Ibsen does not say what happened next. The hope and the crash are left side by side, like The Sun and The Tower in the tail.

People tried to rewrite that ending. In Germany at the time the play had no copyright protection, and theatre managers could change the end to suit their taste. Ibsen, as his translator William Archer tells it, was "driven, under protest, to write an alternative ending": at the last moment the thought of her children keeps Nora at home. He explained that he preferred "to commit the outrage himself, rather than leave his work to the tender mercies of adapters." The patched-up ending soon dropped out of use.

For a 3-19-16 couple this is an important clue. What the author counted as an outrage against his play was not the departure but a home where everything stayed as before. The tail does not promise a separation and does not demand one: the play itself decides nothing for its characters. It says something else. Nobody can stay the same in a doll's house; living together has to become a marriage of two grown-ups.

sections.h2: Temperance at the centre: secret thrift and two on one wreck
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's matrix is 14, Temperance, in every couple with the 3-19-16 tail. The centre is the general atmosphere between the partners, what lives inside the couple and is not for show. Waite gives Temperance this list: "Economy, moderation, frugality, management, accommodation." That is the hidden atmosphere of the Helmer home. Torvald calls his wife a little spendthrift, while for years she has kept a secret budget and paid every quarter.

Lisovskaya describes Temperance at a couple's centre through two poles. At the plus the two are close, settle arguments by talking and compromise, and value peace of mind above things. At the minus one keeps giving way while the other does not notice; one saves while the other spends. In the Helmer home the minus is turned inside out: the one who saves is the one taken for a spendthrift. And Torvald tries to tame the tarantella with words of measure: "Slower, slower!"

The play also has a second couple, and it lives precisely in Temperance. The third act opens with them. While the tarantella is danced upstairs, Mrs Linde and Krogstad sit downstairs at that same table in the middle of the room, two people whose lives have already collapsed. "Nils, how would it be if we two shipwrecked people could join forces? … Two on the same piece of wreckage would stand a better chance than each on their own." This couple comes together after the wreck, with open eyes: Mrs Linde knows what people say about Krogstad.

It is she who decides the fate of the secret. Krogstad is ready to take back his letter unopened, and she stops him: "Helmer must know all about it. This unhappy secret must be disclosed; they must have a complete understanding between them, which is impossible with all this concealment and falsehood going on." In the second act the same Mrs Linde mended Nora's Italian costume: "We will easily put that right." Temperance at the centre of a 3-19-16 couple knows how to mend the party costume, and when to stop mending it.

In these couples Temperance at the centre is always the plain sum of the partners' personal centres, with no reduction: 3 + 11 in 45.7% of couples, 6 + 8 in 54.3%. It is not one person giving way to the other, but a blend of two measures.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Lovers or The Devil
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, the road the two are meant to walk together. In couples with the 3-19-16 tail only two cards occur here: The Lovers (6) in 66.1% and The Devil (15) in 33.9%. Both answer the doll's house, from different sides.

For Lisovskaya, The Lovers at the plus is a couple without secrets that decides even small things together. That is the exact opposite of a secret bond. The value here is to choose each other again, this time without hidden accounts.

The Devil in the place of values sounds sterner. Lisovskaya's main idea about this energy in a couple is that "nobody belongs to anybody". At its plus her Devil speaks openly about desires and, with money, keeps to honesty and freedom from debt. In the play The Devil stands at both ends. Torvald admires his wife: "my dearest treasure… all the beauty that is mine, all my very own." At the end Nora gives back the ring: "There must be perfect freedom on both sides. See, here is your ring back. Give me mine." The bond for the debt is the most literal chain in the play. This couple's value is a home where debts are named out loud and nobody owns anybody.

sections.h2: What a search of all dates shows: The Empress from one, The Sun from both
paragraphs: The 3-19-16 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 79 (1.259%), which puts it 26th of the 97 couple tails. Each point of the couple is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22, so the couple's tail is assembled from the partners' personal tails. Only three combinations are possible here: 21-4-10 + 9-15-6 in 46% of these couples, 12-16-4 + 18-3-12 in 44%, 21-7-13 + 9-12-3 in 10%.
Looking at which partner holds which card in their personal centre or personal tail reveals a pattern that repeats the play.

ul: **The Empress is always brought in by one of the two** — in 100% of couples. One partner has her in the personal centre (the partner whose tail is 9-15-6), in the middle of the personal tail (18-3-12) or in the personal karmic task (9-12-3). The card of the home enters the union through one person, by date of birth, not by sex.
**Nobody owns The Sun.** In no combination does 19 stand in either partner's centre or tail. This couple's sunlit happiness is shared and belongs to no one: it appears only when the two are together.

**The Tower belongs to one partner in only 44% of couples** (the partner whose tail is 12-16-4). In the other 56% neither has it. For most couples the collapse the tail leads to is made by the union itself, not by the character of one of the two.

paragraphs: As a personal tail, 3-19-16 does not occur. In a person, The Tower in the karmic task appears in only one tail, 21-10-16, and then the centre is always 5. The combination "The Tower in the task and Temperance at the centre" exists only for two.
The person born on 05.12.1975 has the personal tail 18-3-12 and centre 6. The person born on 14.04.1975 has the personal tail 12-16-4 and centre 8. Add the matching points:

ul: entry to the task: 18 + 12 = 30 → 3, The Empress;
middle of the task: 3 + 16 = 19, The Sun;
main task: 12 + 4 = 16, The Tower;
centre: 6 + 8 = 14, Temperance.

paragraphs: This is exactly the combination in which one partner has The Empress in the middle of the personal tail, the other has The Tower, and their sum is the couple's Sun. This couple's values card is 15, The Devil.

In this couple The Sun also stands in two more spheres of the reading: "How others see the couple" (5 + 14 = 19) and "What connects" (10 + 9 = 19). From outside this is a radiant couple, and it is the light itself that holds them together. The Tower also stands on the point "What to create together" (12 + 4 = 16), which Lisovskaya reads only at its plus. Her Tower at the plus is a couple who build, renovate and make things together. For this couple even what they create together is tied to rebuilding, to a home the two put together anew.
The 3-19-16 tail predicts neither a crisis nor its date. It shows how the home is built and hints at where that home is thin. Here is what moves the story from a doll's house towards a marriage.

ul: **Don't buy the sun on credit.** Agree out loud on what must never be kept quiet in this home: debts, loans, promises to relatives, big expenses.
**Ask instead of waiting for a miracle.** If a deed is needed, say so in words rather than testing love with trouble.
**Now and then, ask: are the two happy, or only merry?** A party does no harm as long as it does not replace a conversation.
**After a blow, don't save the shine.** First the conversation at the table, then the reconciliation for show.
**Each partner keeps a footing outside the home**: work, money, a circle of their own. Then the home is not the only stage, and nobody in it is a doll.
**Start the first serious conversation before a letter starts it.** Eight years is far too long a pause.

paragraphs: If home holds not quarrels but fear, control over every step or threats, that is no longer a matter for the tail. Get help: a local emergency number or a psychologist.

intro: The three numbers in the couple's destiny matrix are three steps of one story:

ul: **Entry to the task — The Empress (3).** The wish the couple brings to the task: a shared, generous home where everyone is well and everything is beautiful.
**Middle of the task — The Sun (19).** How the couple lives the road: in the light, with celebrations, with a joy that both they and their guests can see.
**Main task — The Tower (16).** What the couple has to learn: to withstand a truth that breaks the comfortable picture, and to build the home a second time, on that truth.

intro: This story already has a play. In 1879 Henrik Ibsen wrote A Doll's House, and the three cards appear in it in exactly this order: a Christmas flat full of parcels and a tree, "our sunlit happiness" — the husband's own words — and a letter that drops into a letter-box with a little glass window. The play's last two stage directions are a hope and a crash. In the English translation the hope even flashes like lightning: "A hope flashes across his mind." Then: "The sound of a door shutting is heard from below." The Sun and The Tower.

faq.q: What does the 3-19-16 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail: the entry to the task is The Empress, a shared wish for a generous, beautiful home; the middle is The Sun, life in the light and in celebration; the main task is The Tower, a truth that breaks the comfortable picture. The couple's task is not to shield the home from the blow at any cost, but to learn to talk seriously and to build the home on truth rather than on a stage set.

faq.q: Does the 3-19-16 tail predict a crisis or a break-up?
faq.a: No. The numbers of the matrix do not predict events or dates. The Tower here describes which lesson is hardest for the couple: a comfortable picture can come to matter more than the truth. Even A Doll's House decides nothing for its characters; Ibsen left the ending open.

faq.q: In a 3-19-16 couple, who is Nora and who is Torvald?
faq.a: Either of the two, and often both in turn. Sex plays no part in the calculation, and the roles from the play are kinds of behaviour. One person keeps a secret for the sake of the shared celebration; the other holds the key to the letter-box and waits for a heroic deed. Ibsen himself called the play a question of humanity, not a women's question.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. Among the 97 couple tails, the numbers 3, 16 and 19 occur only in the order 3-19-16. This triple does not occur as a personal tail either: it exists only for a couple.

faq.q: How can a couple find out whether they have the 3-19-16 tail?
faq.a: Two dates of birth are needed. In each personal matrix take the entry of the tail, the middle of the tail and the karmic task, add the matching points of the two partners and reduce any sum over 22. It is simpler to work out compatibility in the calculator: it shows the three cards of the couple's tail straight away.

report: The husband in Ibsen's A Doll's House calls his married life "our sunlit happiness". That same night his wife tells him she has never once been happy in this house: "No, only merry." The whole of the 3-19-16 couple's tail fits between those two lines.

The tail's first two cards are the brightest in the deck. At the entry to the task stands The Empress: a shared wish for a generous, beautiful home where everyone is well. In the middle stands The Sun: life in the light, with celebrations that both the couple and their guests can see. And the main task is The Tower, the card of collapse. The riddle has a clear answer: **this couple's Tower strikes not at love but at the stage set**, at a home where the two are merry but not always truthful. Nora and Torvald Helmer are not "she" and "he" here but two roles: in a couple either partner can take either one, and often both take turns.

In the first year of their marriage Torvald overworked himself and came close to death, and the only hope was a stay in the south. Nora secretly borrowed 4,800 crowns, forging her father's signature, and the year in Italy saved her husband's life. "It was a wonderfully beautiful journey, and it saved Torvald's life." He believes his father-in-law paid. And his golden rule is spoken in the play's first minutes: "No debt, no borrowing." The home the two want to see beautiful stands on a debt, and Nora keeps quiet about it precisely for beauty's sake: "our beautiful happy home would no longer be what it is now." This couple's sun is paid for in instalments, and for years Nora has paid the interest herself.

Worse than the debt are the expectations. Torvald confesses: "I have often wished that you might be threatened by some great danger, so that I might risk my life's blood." Nora waits for "the wonderful thing": her husband will read the creditor's letter and take the forgery on himself. **Both expect a heroic deed against a backdrop of catastrophe, and neither says a word.** This is The Sun at its minus: waiting for heroism instead of talking.

The card also leaves a clue in the numbers. Neither partner has The Sun in their personal centre or personal tail: only the couple gives birth to it. This couple's sunlit happiness is shared and belongs to no one; it appears only when the two are together.

Waite calls The Tower a card of unforeseen catastrophe. In the play the catastrophe is foreseen. Krogstad's letter lies in a letter-box with a little glass window: "you can see it through the glass in the letter-box." — "And your husband keeps the key?" — "Yes, always." For three days both live next to the lightning, while Nora rehearses the tarantella to keep her husband from reaching the box. "My dear darling Nora, you are dancing as if your life depended on it." — "So it does." The Tower of a 3-19-16 couple is often like that: they know about it in advance and dance so that it does not happen today.

Once the letter is read, two images fall in a single evening. Torvald cries: "What a horrible awakening!" — his lark has turned out to be "a hypocrite, a liar". Nora will tell him: "I saw you were not the man I had thought you were." Her knight has fallen too.

After the blow Torvald proposes a plan: to act "as if everything between us were just as before", and to "save the remains, the fragments, the appearance". In the original the last word is skinnet. The Norwegian Academy's dictionary derives it from skína, "to shine": the first sense is light, gleam, as in solskinn, "sunshine"; the second is an outward show that covers a flaw. **After the blow, the couple risks saving the shine instead of the home.**

Then the creditor returns the bond. "I am saved! Nora, I am saved!" — "And I?" — "You too, of course." Torvald throws the paper into the stove and promises that "soon everything will be just as it was before." This is the tail's main failure: the lightning has struck, and the house is rebuilt from the same drawings, with the same roles and the same toy language. Today it looks like this: a debt or a secret comes out, the two make up quickly, book a trip, post a photo together, and never talk about why the secret was needed.

report.h3: "Yes, Torvald, I have changed my things"

report: Nora goes to take off her fancy dress, the same Italian costume she danced in, and comes back in everyday clothes. "Sit down. It will take some time." Then comes the play's key line: "We have been married now eight years. Does it not occur to you that this is the first time we two, you and I, husband and wife, have had a serious conversation?" **The strong Tower for this couple is not a slammed door but a change of clothes and a table**: the sunny costume is off, and the bill that was paid in secret for years lies on the table for the first time.

Ibsen left the ending open. For strangers to become close, "the most wonderful thing of all would have to happen": "Both you and I would have to be so changed that… That our life together would be a real wedlock." For the German stage Ibsen was forced to write another ending, in which Nora stays at home, and he called it an outrage against the play. What he counted as the outrage was not the departure but a home where everything stayed as before. The 3-19-16 tail does not promise a separation. **It says that nobody can stay the same in a doll's house.**
Simple things move the story on:

ul: don't buy the sun on credit: agree out loud on what must never be kept quiet in this home — debts, loans, promises to relatives, big expenses;
don't wait for a miracle; ask in words, without testing love with trouble;
now and then, check whether the two are happy or only merry;
after a blow, first the conversation at the table, then the reconciliation for show.

report: If home holds not quarrels but fear, control over every step or threats, that is no longer a matter for the tail. Help is needed: a local emergency number or crisis line, or a psychologist.

unit.title: Take off the sunny costume

captions.M: To want a generous, beautiful home where all are well
captions.N: To live in light and celebration, silent on what matters
captions.D: To bear the truth and build the home on it, not on shine

unit.meaning: Your task is not to save the shine after a blow, but to sit at the table, talk seriously and build the home on truth.
